---
title: "Case study: choosing a vehicle routing heuristic"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
```

A distribution company plans delivery routes every day with a constructive heuristic for the
capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP): one depot, customers with demands, vehicles with a
capacity. Two classic candidates are

* **A, sweep** (Gillett and Miller, 1974): sort customers by polar angle around the depot and
  fill vehicles in that order;
* **B, savings** (Clarke and Wright, 1964): start with one route per customer and merge routes
  in decreasing order of the distance saved.

Both are followed by 2-opt inside each route. Which one should the company deploy on problems
like its own? This article runs the comparison with `seqbench`. The companion article runs the
same comparison with larger instances on 1,000 resampled streams with a known truth
(`experiments/configs/app_cvrp_2026-10-23.R` in the package repository).

```{r}
library(seqbench)
```

## The heuristics

```{r}
route_len <- function(r, D) { p <- c(1L, r, 1L); sum(D[cbind(p[-length(p)], p[-1])]) }

two_opt <- function(r, D) {
  if (length(r) < 3L) return(r)
  repeat {
    p <- c(1L, r, 1L); k <- length(p); improved <- FALSE
    for (i in 1:(k - 3L)) {
      j <- (i + 2L):(k - 1L)
      delta <- D[p[i], p[j]] + D[p[i + 1L], p[j + 1L]] - D[p[i], p[i + 1L]] - D[cbind(p[j], p[j + 1L])]
      b <- which(delta < -1e-12)
      if (length(b)) { jj <- j[b[1]]; p[(i + 1L):jj] <- rev(p[(i + 1L):jj]); improved <- TRUE; break }
    }
    r <- p[2:(k - 1L)]
    if (!improved) return(r)
  }
}

sweep <- function(xy, q, Q, D) {
  ang <- (atan2(xy[-1, 2] - xy[1, 2], xy[-1, 1] - xy[1, 1]) - runif(1, 0, 2 * pi)) %% (2 * pi)
  routes <- list(); cur <- integer(0); load <- 0
  for (v in order(ang) + 1L) {
    if (load + q[v] > Q) { routes[[length(routes) + 1L]] <- cur; cur <- integer(0); load <- 0 }
    cur <- c(cur, v); load <- load + q[v]
  }
  lapply(c(routes, list(cur)), two_opt, D = D)
}

savings <- function(q, Q, D) {
  n <- nrow(D); cust <- 2:n
  pr <- which(upper.tri(D[cust, cust]), arr.ind = TRUE)
  i <- cust[pr[, 1]]; j <- cust[pr[, 2]]
  s <- D[1, i] + D[1, j] - D[cbind(i, j)]
  o <- order(-s)[s[order(-s)] > 0]; i <- i[o]; j <- j[o]
  rid <- seq_len(n); routes <- as.list(seq_len(n)); load <- q
  for (k in seq_along(i)) {
    a <- i[k]; b <- j[k]; ra <- rid[a]; rb <- rid[b]
    if (ra == rb || load[ra] + load[rb] > Q) next
    A <- routes[[ra]]; B <- routes[[rb]]
    new <- if (A[length(A)] == a && B[1] == b) c(A, B) else if (A[1] == a && B[length(B)] == b) c(B, A)
      else if (A[length(A)] == a && B[length(B)] == b) c(A, rev(B)) else if (A[1] == a && B[1] == b) c(rev(A), B)
      else NULL
    if (is.null(new)) next
    routes[[ra]] <- new; routes[rb] <- list(NULL); load[ra] <- load[ra] + load[rb]; rid[new] <- ra
  }
  lapply(Filter(Negate(is.null), routes[cust]), two_opt, D = D)
}
```

## A bounded loss without truncation

The cost of the optimal solution is unknown, but it is at least the length of a minimum
spanning tree of the depot and customers, and at least the radial bound
`2 * sum(q * d0) / Q`. Call the larger of the two `LB`. The **relative gap**
`1 - LB / z` of a solution of cost `z` lies in `[0, 1)` for every feasible solution, so the
bounds `[0, 1]` hold by construction: no truncation and no clipping.

```{r}
mst_len <- function(D) {
  n <- nrow(D); inT <- c(TRUE, rep(FALSE, n - 1L)); best <- D[1, ]; tot <- 0
  for (k in 2:n) { best[inT] <- Inf; v <- which.min(best); tot <- tot + best[v]; inT[v] <- TRUE; best <- pmin(best, D[v, ]) }
  tot
}

instance <- function() {
  n <- sample(30:80, 1)
  depot <- switch(sample(3, 1), c(0.5, 0.5), c(0, 0), runif(2))
  xy <- rbind(depot, matrix(runif(2 * n), n))
  q <- c(0, sample(1:10, n, replace = TRUE))
  Q <- max(max(q), ceiling(runif(1, 4, 15) * mean(q[-1])))
  D <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
  lb <- max(mst_len(D), 2 * sum(q * D[1, ]) / Q)
  t0 <- proc.time()[["user.self"]]
  za <- sum(vapply(sweep(xy, q, Q, D), route_len, 0, D = D))
  zb <- sum(vapply(savings(q, Q, D), route_len, 0, D = D))
  c(loss_a = 1 - lb / za, loss_b = 1 - lb / zb, cost = proc.time()[["user.self"]] - t0)
}
```

## Design first

The margin is fixed before any instance is run: one percentage point of gap. The budget is
600 instances.

```{r}
design <- comparison_design(alpha = 0.05, margin = 0.01, bounds = c(0, 1),
                            boundary = "betting", n_max = 600)
design
```

## Run instances as they come

The instances are solved in batches of 25, and the comparison is updated after each batch;
the protocol may be inspected at every step without invalidating it.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
state <- initialize_comparison(design)
batch <- 0
while (stopping_decision(state) == "continue") {
  ids <- batch * 25 + 1:25
  rows <- t(replicate(25, instance()))
  state <- suppressWarnings(update_comparison(state,
    data.frame(instance = ids, loss_a = rows[, "loss_a"], loss_b = rows[, "loss_b"], cost = rows[, "cost"])))
  batch <- batch + 1
}
stopping_decision(state)
comparison_report(state)
```

```{r}
ggplot2::autoplot(state)
```

The running confidence sequence for `mean(loss_a - loss_b)` leaves the band `[-0.01, 0.01]`
from above: on random problems like these the savings heuristic closes relevantly more of the
gap to the lower bound than the sweep heuristic. The report records the number of instances,
the CPU time spent, the assumptions and the versions, which is what a reader needs to audit the
decision.

## What the answer means

The estimand is the mean relative gap difference over the **population defined by the
generator**: 30 to 80 customers in the unit square, uniform positions, small integer demands.
A company whose problems look different (clustered customers, time windows, heterogeneous
fleets) should write a generator, or sample past problems, that describes *its* population;
the article's study uses a richer generator with clustered and mixed positions and three demand
profiles. The comparison also says nothing about running time unless it is folded into the
loss; here it is only recorded as cost.
